facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Chand Baori is an architectural wonder with 3,500 perfectly symmetrical, narrow steps.
facts.text: Chand Baori contains approximately 3,500 narrow, symmetrical stone steps engineered into its descending pyramidal terraces.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It has 3500 steps cascading 13 stories deep into a massive tank at the bottom and has been constructed in an upside-down pyramid style.
facts.source_name: Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
facts.text: The stepwell descends across 13 subterranean storeys arranged in an inverted stepped pyramid configuration.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: It extends approximately 30 m (100 ft) into the ground, making it one of the deepest and largest stepwells in India.
facts.text: The vertical excavation of Chand Baori plunges approximately 30 metres into the earth, making it one of the deepest stepwells in India.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The air at the bottom of the well remains 5–6 degrees cooler than at the surface.
facts.text: Due to depth and natural evaporative cooling, the subterranean microclimate at the base of the stepwell stays roughly 5 to 6 degrees cooler than surface ambient temperatures.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Chand Baori is situated 88 kms from Jaipur.
facts.text: The stepwell site is located in Abhaneri village in Dausa district, roughly 88 kilometres from the state capital Jaipur.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: A double flight of steps on three sides takes one to the surface of the water below. The fourth side is a three-storeyed pavilion with intricately carved jharokhas (windows), galleries and balconies meant for the royal family to sit in.
facts.text: Three sides of the quadrangle feature cascading steps to access fluctuating water tables, while the fourth northern side is occupied by multi-tiered royal pavilions and columned galleries.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Abhaneri. Chand Baori.
facts.text: Chand Baori is an ancient monument legally protected and maintained as a monument of national importance by the Archaeological Survey of India.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Adjoining the Chand Baori is the Harshat Mata Temple. This 9th-10th century temple is dedicated to Harshat Mata, who is considered to be the goddess of joy and happiness for the whole village.
facts.text: The adjacent 9th-to-10th-century Harshat Mata Temple preserves religious sculptures that mirror carvings found within the stepwell precinct.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: It was built by King Chanda of the Nikumbha Dynasty in 9th century AD.
facts.text: The patron's identity is disputed among historians, with state tourism records attributing it to King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty while others associate him with the Gurjara-Pratihara or Chauhan lineages.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: However, no epigraphic evidence has been found regarding the construction of the Chand Baori or the adjoining Harshat Mata Temple. Based on similarities in style and carvings with the terraced temples of Paranagar and Mandore, the Baori can be dated to the 8th-9th century.
facts.source_name: Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
facts.text: Art historians estimate the foundation to circa 800 CE through stylistic comparison with Mandore and Paranagar temples, though the site lacks any epigraphic inscription confirming its exact date or patron.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: According to Morna Livingston in Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India, Chand Baori is one of the few stepwells that has 'two classical periods of water building in a single setting'.
facts.source_name: Steps to Water: The Ancient Stepwells of India
facts.text: Scholars debate whether the structure represents a single architectural phase or multi-century development, as Morna Livingston identified 8th-century lower step masonry juxtaposed with 18th-century Mughal-period upper arcades.

sheet.summary: Local folklore maintains that supernatural entities erected Chand Baori overnight, leaving behind an inescapable maze of steps and a vanished wedding procession in secret subterranean caves. Archaeological inspection demonstrates that the structure is a masterwork of hydraulic engineering, featuring 13 storeys, approximately 3,500 symmetrical steps, and subterranean thermal cooling that lowers temperatures by 5 to 6 degrees Celsius. Historians disagree over the dynastic allegiance of the legendary King Chanda and whether the site was completed in the 9th century CE or significantly rebuilt centuries later with Mughal-era pavilions. In the absence of contemporary foundation inscriptions, the exact construction timeline and the specific guild of master masons who drafted its geometry remain unknown.
